title: The Queen of Sheba
hookLine: a wise ruler who consulted and chose well (27:23–44)

lines: A LETTER, DELIVERED BY A BIRD.
cards: A letter lands on a queen's desk. Well, the Qur'an says a bird delivered it. It comes from a king, Sulayman, whose army includes people, jinn and birds.
It tells her not to be proud, and to come to him in submission. Her chiefs remind her how strong they are, and leave the choice with her. Whatever she does next, a whole kingdom will live with it.
Surah an-Naml, the Ant, tells what she did.

teach.h: A WOMAN RULING, A MIGHTY THRONE.
teach.b: First, the hoopoe's report. Verse twenty-three: I found a woman ruling over them, given plenty of everything, and she has a mighty throne. Her people, it adds, worship the sun.
The Qur'an never gives her a name; tradition calls her Bilqis. Then the letter arrives, and watch her. She calls it a noble letter.

teach.h: ADVISE ME: I DECIDE NOTHING ALONE.
teach.b: She gathers her chiefs and says: advise me in my affair; I never decide a matter until you're present. They answer: we have strength and great might, but the command is yours. She doesn't take the bait.
When kings enter a town, she says, they ruin it and humble its noblest people.

teach.h: A GIFT INSTEAD OF A WAR.
teach.b: So instead of war, she sends a gift, and waits to see how the messengers come back. Three wise moves in a row: honor the message, consult, test before you strike. Sulayman refuses the gift.
She comes to him herself. He's had her throne brought ahead, disguised, and she's asked: is your throne like this? Her answer is careful, almost lawyerly: it is as though it were it.
Then a floor of glass she takes for water.
And in verse forty-four, her choice: my Lord, I have wronged myself, and I submit, with Sulayman, to Allah, the Lord of the worlds. With Sulayman, not to him.

Commentators notice that word: she stands beside him before Allah. The Qur'an spends more verses on her reasoning than on her wealth: a ruler who listened, refused a needless war, and chose with her eyes open.

how: Muslims read the Queen of Sheba's story in surah an-Naml; teachers often point to her as an example of consultation (shura) and wise leadership.

o: the name tradition gives the Queen of Sheba
the throne brought to Sulayman in disguise
the hoopoe that carried Sulayman's letter

games.q: the Queen of Sheba — tap the pairs.
p: brought the report of her kingdom
a test instead of a war

s: it never names her; Bilqis is the name from tradition.
she consulted her chiefs before deciding
advise me: I decide nothing until you are present.
she submitted with Sulayman to Allah, the Lord of the worlds.

games.q: you're the queen. your generals say: we have strength and great might, the command is yours. what do you do?
o: send a gift and see how he responds.
games.why: she sends a gift, saying kings who enter a town ruin it. wisdom over a needless war (27:34–35).

practice: Bring to mind one decision in front of you, and walk it through her steps. What is actually being asked of me? Who should I ask before I decide?
Is there a smaller step to test first? Don't decide during the sit; just see which step you'd been skipping.

wordCard.voice: Bilqis. The name tradition gives the Queen of Sheba, who consulted her council, chose a gift over war, and submitted with Sulayman to Allah. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: Saba', Sheba, her kingdom; surah 34 is named after it.

carryVoice: Your line: she chose well. She listened, consulted, and only then chose. Day six hundred seventy-four, done.
